sentences.text: The genus name Ligabueino translates to "Ligabue's little one," honoring the Italian doctor who discovered the fossil.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes a 62 mm femur, pelvic fragments, finger bones, and vertebrae from the neck, back, and tail.
This proportionally short leg indicates that the animal was diminutive.
With an estimated body length of only 79 cm, Ligabueino ranks among the smallest dinosaurs known to date.
Argentine paleontologist José Fernando Bonaparte described the species in 1996 from an extremely fragmentary skeleton found in Neuquén Province.
Despite its small size, the ilium features a well-developed dorsal projection, and unfused vertebral centra suggest the specimen was a juvenile.
Body proportions and hindlimb development suggest cursorial adaptations consistent with an active lifestyle, possibly insectivorous or microcarnivorous.
In 2024, Ligabueino was recovered as a sister taxon to Berthasauridae and Abelisauroidea.
Ligabueino lived during the Early Cretaceous Period, specifically from the Barremian to early Aptian stages.
It inhabited a fluvial system with swampy areas and dense vegetation in what is now Patagonia, sharing the landscape with dinosaurs like Amargasaurus and various titanosauriforms.
Although initially assigned to Noasauridae by Bonaparte in 1996, the phylogenetic position of Ligabueino has been extensively debated.

Later studies by Filippi et al. (2016) using an expanded phylogenetic matrix recovered Ligabueino again as a noasaurid, though in a more derived position than Eoabelisaurus, suggesting it represents an early transitional form within Patagonian ceratosaurians.
